The sulfur TES vessel was designed and fabricated in accordance with ASME Section VIII for pressure vessels, while the internal heat exchanger piping was designed per ASME B31.1, consistent with established industry practices for high-temperature steam generators and boiler systems. Figure 1 shows the engineering drawing of the pilot prototype unit that went through multiple iterations between Element 16 and PCL (fabrication firm) engineering team to ensure that the design of the sulfur TES was ASME code compliant. The final design of the single-tank sulfur TES was informed by the thermophysical properties, corrosion behavior and safety considerations associated with molten sulfur. As discussed earlier, the selected single-tank configuration retains sulfur entirely within the thermal energy storage vessel, rather than pumping it between tanks as in conventional two-tank molten salt systems. This design choice significantly reduces failure modes associated with molten sulfur handling, including wear, leakage, valve failure, and solidification in piping, thereby improving system safety and reliability. From a process safety standpoint, the sulfur inside the vessel is blanketed with inert nitrogen gas and as result there is no oxidizing atmosphere in the vessel. Material selection for the storage vessel and internal components was guided by the corrosion and mechanical durability testing conducted in Task 3. Based on these results, stainless steel 316 was selected as the primary material of construction. The measured corrosion rate in Task 3 was used to determine the corrosion allowance. For the targeted discharge heat rate of 30 (±5) kW and a discharge duration of 14 hours (EOP-B), the required storage capacity was determined to be approximately 420– 490 kWh. For molten sulfur cycled between 210°C and 290°C, a 490-kWh storage capacity requires approximately 21 tons of sulfur. Incorporating a 10% design margin, the Page 61 of 87 DE-EE0009329 Element 16 Technologies, Inc. TES vessel was designed to accommodate up to 23 tons of sulfur. The resulting vessel diameter and length are 72 inches and ~265 inches, respectively with a wall thickness of roughly 0.25 inch, inclusive of corrosion allowance.
